benchmark_type_evidence: We build a reading comprehension dataset, BoolQ, of such questions
brief_description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with Wikipedia passages. Questions are gathered from anonymized Google search queries and annotated by humans following the Natural Questions pipeline.

datasets.annotation_method: Human annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) decide if question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, factual), (2) find a passage within the Wikipedia document containing enough information to answer the question, (3) mark whether the answer is yes or no. Questions sourced from anonymized Google search queries filtered for yes/no questions.

data_creator_info.creator_affiliation: Google AI Language / University of Washington
data_creator_info.evidence: Paper states 'We gather data using the pipeline from NQ (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019)' and refers to 'a human annotator' and 'annotators' but does not specify annotator type (crowdworker, professional, etc.) or demographics. Three of the paper authors performed quality assessment on 110 examples. Questions are from Google search users; annotation follows the NQ pipeline.

datasets.notes: 16,000 total examples (13k new + 3k from Natural Questions). Split: 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, 3.2k test. 62.31% 'yes' answers in train set. Average question length 8.9 tokens, average passage length 108 tokens. Human accuracy: 90%.

translated.evidence: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine (Section 3.1). Passages are from Wikipedia. No translation is involved.

native_annotators.evidence: INSUFFICIENT_INFO: Paper states 'We gather data using the pipeline from NQ' and refers to 'a human annotator' and 'annotators' (Section 3.1) but does not specify whether annotators are native English speakers. Three authors (affiliated with Google AI Language and University of Washington) labeled 110 examples for quality assessment (Section 3.3).

culturally_grounded.evidence: Questions are naturally occurring Google search queries and passages are from English Wikipedia. The dataset reflects general English-language internet users' questions and Wikipedia content, not designed with specific cultural grounding in mind (Section 3.1, Section 3.4).

BoolQ.annotation_quality_notes: Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples as gold standard. Answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Of the 10% disagreements, six were ambiguous/debatable cases and five were annotator errors. Singly-annotated examples used for train/dev/test sets (Section 3.3).

datasets_from_scratch_no_english_source.evidence: BoolQ is an English-only dataset. Questions come from English Google search queries and passages from English Wikipedia.

datasets_translated_from_english.evidence: No translation is involved; the dataset is natively English.

all_annotators_native_speakers.evidence: Paper describes annotators following the NQ pipeline (Section 3.1) but provides no demographic or language proficiency information about annotators.

annotator_workforce.evidence: Paper states 'We gather data using the pipeline from NQ (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019)' (Section 3.1). Three paper authors performed quality assessment on 110 examples (Section 3.3). No information on annotator demographics, compensation, or ethics review is provided.

cultural_flags.english_centricity_notes: BoolQ is an English-only dataset. All questions come from English Google search queries and all passages are from English Wikipedia. The benchmark does not address any non-English languages.

geographic_representation.evidence: Questions are from anonymized Google search queries (likely predominantly English-speaking users). Passages are from English Wikipedia. No geographic diversity is intended or claimed.
